articles.title: Dissenting Parents' Defamation Claim Over School's Allegations of Racism Can Go Forward
articles.content:
北卡罗来纳州最高法院在一项由法官理查德·迪茨主笔、最高法院首席法官保罗·纽比以及法官菲利普·伯格尔二世、塔玛拉·巴林杰和特雷·艾伦共同签署的判决中，审理了土尔宾诉夏洛特拉丁学校案件的部分内容。根据本案起诉书，原告道格和尼古拉·土尔宾将他们的孩子送往私立学校夏洛特拉丁学校。从2020年夏天开始，该校开始改变课程，重点关注种族和性别认同等政治化问题。土尔宾夫妇后来得知，该校向六年级的孩子教授诸如"共和党人是白人至上主义者"等极端言论，并且强迫年轻学生阅读不适合其年龄的关于性别和性别认同的书籍。

2021年，土尔宾夫妇开始与其他家长组织起来，表达对学校课程的担忧。最终，土尔宾夫妇与学校管理层安排了一次会议。然而，学校对土尔宾夫妇的担忧不感兴趣，反而终止了他们的入学合同，并未经事先警告就驱逐了他们的孩子。

土尔宾夫妇以诽谤等罪名起诉该校，法院允许案件继续进行。土尔宾夫妇指控夏洛特拉丁学校和巴德基在第三方面前做出了关于他们PowerPoint演示文稿内容的虚假陈述——具体来说，PowerPoint中包含了种族主义的声称，即少数族裔学生和教职员工"未能通过自己的努力获得他们的职位和荣誉"，这些少数族裔学生和教职员工"不如白人学生和教职员工具有同等的价值"。

夏洛特拉丁学校的诽谤性陈述并未准确描述PowerPoint演示文稿的"要点"或"核心"。首先，演示文稿中唯一提到学校方法如何"侵蚀学生质量"和"教师质量"的部分明确涉及所有学生和教职员工，无论肤色如何。该部分演示文稿指出，对"DEI和批判理论"的过度关注正使学校从传统教育中远离"客观性"、"科学"、"经典读物"等，转而拥抱"政治和意识形态议程"。

当一所长期专注于传统教育重要性的学校转向党派化、政治化的课程时，正如PowerPoint演示文稿所称，这种转变对每个学生和每个教师的影响是相同的。演示文稿中的任何内容都没有表明学校变更课程或意识形态议程对少数族裔学生和教职员工产生了负面影响，而对白人同行则没有影响。

上诉法院审查的PowerPoint演示文稿的剩余部分是对非实力招聘或录取实践的批评，以及呼吁回归"实力社会"。重要的是，这些陈述并没有提到特定学生或学生群体的质量或价值。这些陈述只是主张学校应致力于实力社会，其驱动目标是"学术卓越"。

如果我们采纳上诉法院关于这些陈述的论证，那么任何批评非实力招聘或录取实践的陈述，在法律上就是一种陈述，即从这些实践中受益的人否则不会根据实力获得资格。这是一种谬论。从非实力因素中受益的人仍然可以基于实力获得资格。额外因素的存在并不说明候选人的实力资格。

简单来说，批评所谓的"DEI目标"或招聘和录取中的种族意识标准，并倡导回归"实力社会"，并不等同于声称少数族裔学生和教职员工未能通过自己的努力获得职位和荣誉，或不如其他学生具有同等的价值。我们不同意法律上这些两类评论的"要点"或"核心"相同。后者——聚焦于少数族裔学生或教职员工的所谓劣势的陈述——是有害的和种族主义的。这些攻击性陈述如果被他人听到，可能会损害一个人的声誉和好名。因此，在适当的情况下，声称某人做出这种攻击性陈述而实际上并未这样做，可能构成诽谤。考虑到起诉书中的所有指控，这是其中一个案例。

学校并没有做出"土尔宾夫妇是种族主义者"这样的主观意见陈述。学校向其整个学生、家长和教职员工社区宣称，土尔宾夫妇说了一个具体的种族主义言论。这个说法有一个客观答案：土尔宾夫妇要么说，要么没说。正确的比喻不是说某人是种族主义者，如反对意见中援引的案例，而是说某人使用了种族谩骂。如果这是一个谎言，它就是诽谤。

正如我们在本案具有争议的其他事实指控中所做的那样，我们再次指出，事实可能比起诉书中指控的更多。例如，我们尚不知道演示人员在展示PowerPoint文件时说了什么。在本案的这个阶段，我们只能看文件本身。学校的电子邮件和巴德基的陈述在更广泛的背景下可能涉及超出PowerPoint文件范围的事项。

法院在起诉阶段不能寻求这种全面的背景。这就是事实调查的目的。在本案的这个早期阶段，我们以起诉书中的指控为真，并对土尔宾夫妇做出所有合理的推论。在这里这样做，土尔宾夫妇已经足够指控被告做出了实质性虚假陈述。因此，我们拒绝上诉法院关于虚假性的论证。

正义艾莉森·里格斯，与正义阿尼塔·厄尔斯一起，对这一问题提出了不同的意见，摘录如下：

关于种族主义的指控，像许多主观观点一样，取决于观察者的视角，并不完全符合虚假性测试。原告如何证明声称他表达了特定观点的陈述是虚假的？被告如何证明这是真实的？……许多其他司法管辖区的法院在面对基于种族主义或偏见指控的诽谤索赔案时，认为这些陈述是不可诉的意见表达。

多数派未能分析所指控的诽谤性陈述是事实（可以是虚假的）还是意见（不能是虚假的）。土尔宾夫妇抱怨并推断学校参考他们的电子邮件中，家长们抱怨"多元化的学生和教职员工未能通过自己的努力获得夏洛特拉丁学校的职位和荣誉，多元化是以牺牲卓越为代价的"。

将这种实际陈述，即学校反对的价值观和意见的反映，与"声称某人使用了种族谩骂"相提并论是错误的。相反，土尔宾夫妇诽谤索赔的核心是，夏洛特拉丁学校在描述"重新关注拉丁"演示时，以负面的角度描绘了他们。这是一种完全主观的推论，不适用于虚假性分析。即使在低通知起诉标准下，土尔宾夫妇也必须提出一个具有法律意义的索赔——如果指控的诽谤性陈述是无法证明虚假的意见，他们就无法这样做。

从法律上讲，种族主义指控应该被视为无法证明的意见，而不是事实，如其他司法管辖区所做的那样。例如，史蒂文斯诉蒂尔曼（第七巡回法院，1988年）案中，法院认为种族主义指控"除非它隐含存在未披露的、诽谤性的事实，否则不构成诉讼"；墨菲诉罗森（康涅狄格州，2025年）案中，法院与"许多其他司法管辖区"一道，认为指控某人是"白人至上主义者"是"无法客观验证的"，因此是不可诉的意见；库辛斯诉古迪尔（特拉华州，2022年）案中，法院认为种族主义指控"无法证明虚假"，并且"第一修正案明确规定，[确定什么是种族主义者的含义]将与我们的角色相背离"……我担心这种对使用州诽谤法限制自由言论的限制的表面处理，将对重要的公共辩论产生显著的冷却效应，并将法院大门向应通过公开、公共讨论解决的争议敞开。

法院还允许家长的另一项违约和欺诈索赔继续进行。
articles.summary:
Some excerpts from the long Turpin v. Charlotte Latin Schools, Inc., decided today by the N.C. Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Richard Dietz, joined by Chief Justice Paul Newby and Justices Philip Berger Jr., Tamara Barringer, and Trey Allen:

According to the complaint in this case, Plaintiffs Doug and Nicole Turpin sent their children to a private school called Charlotte Latin School. Beginning in the summer of 2020, the school began to change its curriculum to focus on politicized issues of race and gender identity. At some point, the Turpins learned that the school was teaching their sixth-grade child various polarizing concepts such as "Republicans are white supremacists." The school also required young students to read books on sexuality and gender identity that were not age appropriate.

The Turpins started organizing with other parents to voice their concerns about the school curriculum in 2021. Eventually, the Turpins scheduled a meeting with school leadership. At the meeting, the school was not interested in discussing the Turpins' concerns. Instead, the school terminated the Turpins' enrollment contracts and expelled their children with no advance warning.

Among other things, the Turpins sued the school for defamation, and the court allowed the case to go forward:

The Turpins allege that Charlotte Latin and Baldecchi made false statements [to third parties] about the contents of the [Turpins'] PowerPoint presentation [that the Turpins delivered at the meeting]—specifically, that the PowerPoint contained the racist assertion that minority students and faculty at the school "have not earned their positions and honors" and that those minority students and faculty were "not up to the merit of the school" like the white students and faculty ….

The defamatory statements by Charlotte Latin do not accurately characterize the "gist" or "sting" of the PowerPoint discussion. First, the only portion of the presentation referencing how the school's approach "erodes the quality of student" and the "quality of teacher" expressly addresses all students and faculty, regardless of color. That section of the presentation asserted that the excessive focus on "DEI and Critical Theory" was shifting the school away from a classical education teaching "objectivity," "science," "canonical reading," and so on, to instead embrace a "political and ideological agenda."

When a school that was long focused on the importance of a classical education instead shifts toward a partisan, politicized curriculum, as the PowerPoint claimed, that shift impacts every student and every teacher equally. Nothing in these statements suggests the school's changed curriculum or ideological agenda negatively impacted minority students and faculty but not their white counterparts.

The remaining portions of the PowerPoint examined by the Court of Appeals are critiques of non-merit-based hiring or admissions practices and a pitch to return to a "meritocracy." Importantly, none of these statements refer to the quality or merit of particular students or groups of students. The statements simply assert that the school should commit to a meritocracy where the driving goal is "academic excellence."

Were we to adopt the Court of Appeals' reasoning with respect to these statements, it would mean any statement criticizing non-merit-based hiring or admissions practices is, as a matter of law, a statement that people who benefited from those practices would not otherwise qualify based on merit. This is a fallacy. Someone who benefits from a non-merit-based factor can still be qualified based on merit alone. The presence of that additional factor says nothing about the merit-based qualifications of the candidate.

Simply put, criticizing so-called "DEI goals" or other race-conscious criteria in hiring and admissions, and urging a return to a "meritocracy," is not the equivalent of claiming that minority students and faculty have not earned their positions and honors or are not up to the merit of other students. We do not agree that "the gist" or "the sting" of these two categories of comments are the same as a matter of law. The latter—statements focused on the purported inferiority of minority students or faculty—are pernicious and racist. They are the sort of offensive statements that, if heard by others, can damage one's reputation and good name. Accordingly, in appropriate contexts, claiming that someone made this kind of offensive statement when they did not can be defamatory. Taking as true all the allegations in the complaint, this is one of those cases….

The school did not make a subjective statement of opinion such as "the Turpins are racists." The school told its entire community of students, parents, and faculty that the Turpins said a specific racist thing. That claim has an objective answer: the Turpins either said it or they didn't. The correct analogy is not claiming someone is a racist, as in the cases the dissent cites, but claiming someone used a racial epithet. If that is a lie, it is defamatory.

As we have done with respect to other factual allegations in this divisive case, we again point out that there may be more going on factually than what is alleged in the complaint. For example, we do not yet know what the presenters said as they displayed the PowerPoint document. At this stage of the case, we can look only at the document itself. Both the school's email and Baldecchi's statements may, in full context, have been addressing matters beyond the PowerPoint document.

Courts cannot seek out this sort of full context at the pleadings stage. That is the purpose of fact discovery. At this early stage of the case, we take the allegations in the complaint as true and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the Turpins. Doing so here, the Turpins have sufficiently alleged that defendants made materially false statements. We therefore reject the reasoning of the Court of Appeals with respect to falsity….

Justice Allison Riggs, joined by Justice Anita Earls, dissented with regard to this; an excerpt:

[A]llegations of racism, like many subjective viewpoints, are in the eye of the beholder and do not squarely fit into the falsity test. How could a plaintiff prove that a statement alleging he expressed a particular viewpoint is false? How can a defendant prove that it is true? … "… [M]any courts in other jurisdictions that have faced the issue of defamation claims based on accusations of bigotry or racism have held the statements to be nonactionable statements of opinion." …

The majority fails to analyze whether the alleged defamatory statement is a fact, which can be false, or an opinion, which cannot. Charlotte Latin's email, about which the Turpins complain and that they infer is made in reference to them, states that parents complained "that diverse students and faculty have not earned their positions and honors at Latin and that diversity comes at the expense of excellence."

It is a faulty equivalence to suggest this actual statement, a reflection of values and opinion that the school rejected, is more like "claiming someone used a racial epithet" than "claiming someone is a racist." Instead, the crux of the Turpins' defamation claim is that Charlotte Latin, in characterizing the Refocus Latin presentation, portrayed them in a negative light. This is an entirely subjective inference, which does not lend itself to the falsity analysis. Even with the low notice pleading standard, the Turpins must state a legally cognizable claim—which they cannot do if the alleged defamatory statement is an opinion incapable of falsity.

As a matter of law, allegations of racism should be treated as unprovable opinion, not fact, as they are in other jurisdictions. See, e.g., Stevens v. Tilman (7th Cir. 1988) (holding that an allegation of racism "is not actionable unless it implies the existence of undisclosed, defamatory facts"); Murphy v. Rosen (Conn. 2025) (joining "numerous other jurisdictions" to hold that an allegation a person was a "white supremacist" was "not objectively verifiable" so was a non-actionable opinion); Cousins v. Goodier (Del. 2022) (holding that an allegation of racism was not "provably false" and that "the First Amendment is clear that [determining what it means to be racist] would be the opposite of our role")…. I fear this superficial treatment of the limitations on the use of state defamation law to constrain free speech will have significant chilling effects on important public discourse and will fling open the courthouse doors to disputes that should be settled in open, public conversations, not by judges….

The court also allowed parents' separate breach of contract and fraud claims to go forward.

The post Dissenting Parents' Defamation Claim Over School's Allegations of Racism Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: Fraud Claim Over "No Blowback" Assurance by Private School to Complaining Parents, Followed by Children's Expulsions, Can Go Forward
articles.content:
新浪教育讯 北卡罗来纳州最高法院近日就Turpin诉Charlotte Latin学校一案做出判决，法官理查德·迪茨撰写了多数意见，首席大法官保罗·纽比以及法官菲利普·伯格、塔马拉·巴林格尔和特雷·艾伦共同参与。判决文摘要如下：

原告道格和尼古拉·图宾夫妇将孩子送入私立学校夏洛特拉丁学校就读。据原告诉状称，2020年夏季开始，该校开始调整课程，将种族和性别认同等政治化议题纳入教学内容。图宾夫妇得知，学校向其六年级孩子灌输了"共和党人是白人至上主义者"等极端观点，并要求低年级学生阅读涉及性别认同的不适龄读物。

2021年，图宾夫妇开始与其他家长组织起来，表达对学校课程的担忧。最终，他们安排了与校方领导的会面。然而，校方不仅拒绝讨论家长的关切，还当场解除了图宾夫妇的入学合同，并立即开除其子女，事先未做任何提前通知。

家长们随后提起诉讼，其中包括欺诈指控。法院认为该项指控可以继续审理。多数意见分析指出，欺诈指控需满足五要素：1）虚假陈述或隐瞒重大事实；2）足以欺骗的陈述；3）具有欺骗意图；4）确实造成欺骗；5）给受害方造成损害。原告指控称，夏洛特拉丁学校承诺若家长与校方领导讨论关切问题，将不会有"反弹"或"报复"，但该承诺虚假，校方从一开始就试图欺骗家长，诱使他们参加会议以制造开除子女的借口。家长因此相信校方的承诺，坦诚表达了关切，校方却在同一会议上开除了孩子，如其所愿，尽管事先承诺不会这样做，这种欺骗行为给家长造成了严重损害。

诉状中这些陈述符合通知状告的要求。上诉法院曾认为，电子邮件中的内容已经推翻了欺诈指控。上诉法院解释称，所谓的虚假陈述出现在图宾夫妇请求与校方领导讨论课程时的回复邮件中："我们的教师不会报复，不会有反弹，我向您保证。"上诉法院认为，这句承诺仅指教师不会对原告的孩子进行反弹，而孩子被开除是因为校方终止了原告与被告的入学合同，并非教师的报复行为。

然而，这一逻辑颠覆了审查标准。在审理12(b)(6)动议时，法院应将诉状中的事实陈述视为真实，并以最有利于原告的角度审视。从最有利于图宾夫妇的角度来看，邮件中的"无反弹"承诺远不止上诉法院所理解的那么狭窄。显然，这个"无反弹"的承诺包括不终止图宾家庭的入学合同，不开除孩子。

这一讨论始于图宾夫妇通过电子邮件联系校方领导，询问其六年级孩子的人文课程内容。图宾夫妇解释说，人文课教师向学生教授"共和党是白人至上主义者"，以及"共和党所代表的是种族压迫和白人至上主义的实践"。他们还列举了该课程中许多"左翼进步"议题，认为这些内容过于政治化，不适合六年级学生。在请求与校方领导讨论关切问题时，他们特别强调不希望孩子因他们的投诉而遭受任何反弹。

在回复邮件中，校方表示教师"不会报复"，并承诺"不会有反弹，我向您保证"。在上下文中，理解"无反弹"不仅指教师不会在课堂上报复，更是合理的。校方在邮件中明确表示，教师不会报复，且不会有反弹，合理人士可能会将这两者理解为不同的事情。

更根本的是，根据普通英语的用法，当家长希望与校方领导讨论敏感问题，但警告不想让孩子"因我们提出的问题而遭受任何可能的反弹"时，校方管理人员回复"不会有反弹，我向您保证"，合理理解这保证包括不将孩子从学校开除。因此，在正确应用审查标准并从最有利于图宾夫妇而非学校的角度审视这些陈述及其合理推论时，"无反弹"的保证超出了仅承诺教师不会报复的范围。

法院还允许家长的单独违约和诽谤指控继续审理，理由不同。
articles.summary:
Some excerpts from the long Turpin v. Charlotte Latin Schools, Inc., decided today by the N.C. Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Richard Dietz, joined by Chief Justice Paul Newby and Justices Philip Berger Jr., Tamara Barringer, and Trey Allen:

According to the complaint in this case, Plaintiffs Doug and Nicole Turpin sent their children to a private school called Charlotte Latin School. Beginning in the summer of 2020, the school began to change its curriculum to focus on politicized issues of race and gender identity. At some point, the Turpins learned that the school was teaching their sixth-grade child various polarizing concepts such as "Republicans are white supremacists." The school also required young students to read books on sexuality and gender identity that were not age appropriate.

The Turpins started organizing with other parents to voice their concerns about the school curriculum in 2021. Eventually, the Turpins scheduled a meeting with school leadership. At the meeting, the school was not interested in discussing the Turpins' concerns. Instead, the school terminated the Turpins' enrollment contracts and expelled their children with no advance warning….

The parents sued for, among other things, fraud, and the court let the claim go forward; here's the majority's analysis (the partial dissent doesn't focus on the particular "no blowback" statement that the majority discusses here):

To bring a claim for fraud, a plaintiff must allege a "(1) false representation or concealment of a material fact, (2) reasonably calculated to deceive, (3) made with intent to deceive, (4) which does in fact deceive, (5) resulting in damage to the injured party." …

Here, the complaint alleges that Charlotte Latin promised the Turpins there would be no "blowback" or "retaliation" against them or their children if they met with school leadership to discuss their concerns; that this promise was false and, from the beginning, Charlotte Latin intended to deceive the Turpins and lure them to the meeting in order to create a pretext for expelling the children; that the Turpins believed Charlotte Latin's promise and spoke openly about their concerns because they believed the school would not use those discussions as the pretextual grounds to expel the children; that the school, in that same meeting, expelled the children, as they intended from the outset, despite promising the Turpins they would not do so; and that the school's deceit caused significant damage to the Turpins.

Again, as with the contract claim, these allegations on their face satisfy the requirements of notice pleading….

The Court of Appeals held that facts disclosed in the emails necessarily defeated the fraud claim. The court explained that the allegedly fraudulent statement is contained in a series of emails where the Turpins asked to meet school leadership to discuss the curriculum for one of their children's classes. The allegedly false statement is this sentence in a response email from Charlotte Latin to the Turpins: "Our teachers do not retaliate and there will be no blowback, I assure you."

This statement, according to the Court of Appeals, only promised no "blowback from the teacher towards plaintiffs' child." That blowback from the teacher did not occur, the court reasoned, because the child's "removal from the school was an ancillary effect of the termination of the enrollment contract between plaintiffs and defendants," not a retaliatory action by "a teacher."

This reasoning turns the standard of review on its head. "When reviewing a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, we treat the complaint's factual allegations as true and view them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff." Viewed in the light most favorable to the Turpins, the promise of no "blowback" contained in the email is not nearly as narrow as the Court of Appeals interpreted it. Instead, that promise of "no blowback" plainly included a promise not to terminate the Turpins' enrollment contract and kick the child out of school.

This discussion began with the Turpins emailing school leadership about one of their children, a sixth grader taking a humanities class. The Turpins explained that the humanities teacher taught the students that "Republicans are white supremacists" and that "what Republicans stand for is racial suppression and white supremacy in action." The Turpins also recounted many other "left wing progressive" topics in the course that they believed were wrongly politicized and inappropriate for a sixth grader. When asking to meet with school leadership to discuss their concerns, the Turpins emphasized that they did not want their child "to experience any possible blowback because of what we are bringing to your attention":

I wanted to discuss with you a situation that is of serious concern to Nicole and I at your convenience. I would prefer that we discuss this situation on a call, before you address this with the teacher I am referencing in this email. We do not want [our child] to experience any possible blowback because of what we are bringing to your attention.

In response to this email, the school stated that its teachers "do not retaliate" and that "there will be no blowback, I assure you":

Thank you for the email. You make some serious claims that I need to investigate with the teacher, which is only fair so she can provide context. Our teachers do not retaliate and there will be no blowback, I assure you. Please give me a day or two to look into it and will get back to you shortly.

It is entirely reasonable to view the meaning of the term "no blowback" in this context to mean more than just retaliation by the teacher in the classroom. After all, the school's email expressly assured the Turpins both that there would be no retaliation from the teacher and that there would be no blowback, which a reasonable person certainly could interpret as being two separate things.

But even more fundamentally, in ordinary English usage, when parents want to discuss a sensitive topic with school administrators but caution that they do not want their child to "experience any possible blowback because of what we are bringing to your attention," and the school administrator responds with "there will be no blowback, I assure you," it is quite reasonable to understand the assurance of "no blowback" to include terminating the child's enrollment at school. Thus, when we properly apply the standard of review and view this allegation and all its reasonable inferences in the Turpins' favor, not the school's, the assurance went beyond a promise of no blowback from the teacher alone….

The court also allowed parents' separate breach of contract and defamation claims to go forward.on different grounds.

The post Fraud Claim Over "No Blowback" Assurance by Private School to Complaining Parents, Followed by Children's Expulsions, Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason.com.

北卡罗来纳州最高法院近日在特宾诉夏洛特拉丁学校案（Turpin v. Charlotte Latin Schools, Inc.）中作出裁决，法官理查德·迪茨（Richard Dietz）撰写的判决书由首席法官保罗·纽比（Paul Newby）及法官菲利普·伯格二世（Philip Berger Jr.）、塔玛拉·巴林杰（Tamara Barringer）和特雷·艾伦（Trey Allen）共同支持。

原告道格和尼科尔·特宾（Doug and Nicole Turpin）曾将子女送到私立学校夏洛特拉丁学校就读。根据原告起诉书，该校从2020年夏季开始，将课程重点转向种族和性别认同等政治化议题。特宾夫妇得知，学校在教导其六年级子女时传授诸如"共和党人是白人至上主义者"等极端观点。此外，学校还要求年幼学生阅读与年龄不符的性别认同和性教育书籍。

2021年，特宾夫妇开始与其他家长联合，就学校课程内容提出质疑。最终，特宾夫妇与校方领导会面，校方不仅不愿讨论特宾夫妇的顾虑，反而在未事先告知的情况下终止了特宾夫妇的入学合同并开除了其子女。

本案涉及当前社会争议话题，但法院强调，这些争议与本案法律问题无关。法院的职责是判断特宾夫妇的起诉书是否符合民事诉讼中的"通知起诉"标准，即起诉书应包含简明的陈述，足以通知被告导致诉讼的事件或交易。审查起诉书时，法院应将所有陈述视为真实，除非确定原告无法提供任何事实支持其诉求。

判决书核心部分分析了特宾夫妇的违约诉求。合同终止条款允许夏洛特拉丁学校在以下两种情况下终止学生入学：1）家长行为使学校与家长之间的"积极合作关系"变得不可能；2）家长行为"严重干扰"学校的使命。特宾夫妇主张，学校违反了该终止条款并构成违约。特宾夫妇陈述的事实是：学校声称因其行为导致合作关系不再可能或严重干扰学校使命而开除学生，但实际上学校并不真正相信这一点。特宾夫妇认为，学校以合同条款为假借口，实际开除原因与合同规定不符。

值得注意的是，夏洛特拉丁学校在庭审中承认，如果学校出于恶意或假借口终止合同，那么确实构成违约。特宾夫妇的起诉书明确指出，学校出于恶意，清楚地知道终止条款并未真正被满足，但仍然选择以假借口开除学生。这是特宾夫妇起诉书的核心事实主题——他们主张学校知道特宾夫妇的行为是合作和尊敬的，也知道他们的观点并未干扰学校的使命，但学校仍坚持出于其他原因报复他们，并以合同条款为假借口。

在"通知起诉"标准下，特宾夫妇的起诉书满足了进入审理阶段的要求。特宾夫妇无法事先知道学校的真实意图，因为要想入人之心，他们需具备读心术。这种涉及当事人主观意图的事实主张，在起诉阶段无法完全阐明，但可以概括陈述。特宾夫妇的起诉书包含了许多关于假借口的可能解释，例如学校受到"取消文化"（cancel culture）的影响，并担心如果不开除特宾夫妇，自己可能会被"取消"。

法官艾莉森·里格斯（Allison Riggs）和安妮塔·厄尔斯（Anita Earls）提出部分不同意见。他们认为，学校与家长的合同赋予学校"近乎不受限制的终止学生入学的自由裁量权"。合同明确规定，学生就读于该校是一种特权而非权利，学校保留基于家长行为而随时终止学生入学的权利。不同意见指出，私立学校的合同条款赋予学校广泛的终止权，家长可选择接受或拒绝这些条款，或选择其他学校。只要不违反法律或公共政策，私立学校可以基于政治意识形态终止入学，家长不满意的话，可以选择其他学校或公立学校。不同意见认为，即使学校终止入学的理由是假借口，学校仍有权基于合同赋予的广泛自由裁量权行事。

法院还允许家长关于欺诈和诽谤的单独诉求进入审理阶段。特宾夫妇的代表律师包括克里斯托弗·S·爱德华兹（Christopher S. Edwards）、亚历克斯·C·戴尔（Alex C. Dale）、亚历山德拉·E·费里（Alexandra E. Ferri）和乔纳森·A·沃格尔（Jonathan A. Vogel）。
articles.summary:
Some excerpts from the long Turpin v. Charlotte Latin Schools, Inc., decided today by the N.C. Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Richard Dietz, joined by Chief Justice Paul Newby and Justices Philip Berger Jr., Tamara Barringer, and Trey Allen:

According to the complaint in this case, Plaintiffs Doug and Nicole Turpin sent their children to a private school called Charlotte Latin School. Beginning in the summer of 2020, the school began to change its curriculum to focus on politicized issues of race and gender identity. At some point, the Turpins learned that the school was teaching their sixth-grade child various polarizing concepts such as "Republicans are white supremacists." The school also required young students to read books on sexuality and gender identity that were not age appropriate.

The Turpins started organizing with other parents to voice their concerns about the school curriculum in 2021. Eventually, the Turpins scheduled a meeting with school leadership. At the meeting, the school was not interested in discussing the Turpins' concerns. Instead, the school terminated the Turpins' enrollment contracts and expelled their children with no advance warning….

The subject matter of this lawsuit no doubt touches on divisive topics in contemporary social discourse. But none of those divisive topics have any bearing on the legal issues before this Court today. Our task is to determine if the Turpins' complaint satisfies the "notice pleading" standard that applies in civil cases. That well-settled standard requires the complaint to contain a "short and plain statement" sufficient to notify the defendants of "the events or transactions which produced the claim." When reviewing a complaint under this standard, courts must take all the allegations as true and cannot grant a motion to dismiss unless it "appears certain that plaintiffs could prove no set of facts which would entitle them to relief." …

There's a lot going on in the 16K words of opinions, but here's the heart of the analysis allowing Turpins' breach of contract claim to go forward:

[T]he crux of this contract claim is a termination clause permitting Charlotte Latin to end enrollment if one of two contractual criteria is satisfied…. The termination provision permits Charlotte Latin to "discontinue enrollment" whenever it determines that one of two criteria is satisfied: (1) a parent's actions make a "positive, collaborative working relationship" with the school impossible or (2) the parent's actions "seriously interfere" with the school's mission:

A positive, collaborative working relationship between the School and a student's parent/guardians is essential to the fulfillment of the School's mission. Therefore, the School reserves the right to discontinue enrollment if it concludes that the actions of a parent/guardian make such a relationship impossible or seriously interfere with the School's mission.

The Turpins allege that the school violated this termination provision and, as a result, breached the contract. Their factual allegations are straightforward: Charlotte Latin claimed to be expelling the students under this termination clause because the Turpins made a collaborative relationship impossible or were seriously interfering with the school's mission. But, according to the complaint, Charlotte Latin didn't actually believe that. The Turpins allege that the school decided to expel their children for reasons that were not permitted by the contract and then used the contractual grounds as a false pretext.

Importantly, even Charlotte Latin concedes that, if this were true—that is, if the school acted under a false pretext—it would be a breach of the contract. In their briefing, the school acknowledged that the Turpins could state a claim based on "allegations of some improper pretext on Latin's part—such as an attempt to get out of a bad deal." And at oral argument, Charlotte Latin again conceded that the termination clause "may not be invoked with a pretext or in bad faith."

This is precisely what the complaint alleges. The Turpins contend that the school acted under a false pretext and knew that the termination criteria were not actually satisfied. That is the core factual theme of the Turpins' lengthy complaint—they allege that Charlotte Latin knew the Turpins were being collaborative and respectful and knew that their views did not interfere with the mission of a school whose very name invokes a focus on the classical traditions of discourse, rationality, and critical thinking. But, the Turpins allege, the school was determined to retaliate against them for other reasons and used the contractual grounds as the false pretext to do so….

Thus, under the "notice pleading" standard described above, the Turpins have stated a claim that moves past the pleading stage….

Of course, the Turpins cannot yet know the real reason behind the pretext. How could they? Are they mind-readers? … This is precisely why these types of factual allegations, concerning something in the mind of the defendant, cannot be fully explained at the pleading stage. Instead, "intent, knowledge, and other condition of mind of a person may be averred generally." That is what the Turpins did here.

It is worth noting, as well, that the complaint does contain many possible explanations for the false pretext…. [T]o point out just one obvious explanation contained in the complaint, … [t]he Turpins allege that the school was infected by "what has come to be known in American society as 'cancel culture.'" They further allege that they chose to stand up to that "cancel culture" movement and formed the Refocus Latin group to challenge it. One can readily infer from the complaint that one possible reason for the school's pretext was that leadership had to "cancel" the Turpins, as they allege, because school officials were fearful that if they didn't find a way to cancel the Turpins, they might be canceled themselves….

Justice Allison Riggs, joined by Justice Anita Earls, dissented in relevant part; to summarize (and necessarily oversimplify) a long opinion, the dissent took the view that the school's contracts with the parents gave the school "near unfettered discretion to terminate a student's enrollment":

[T]he Enrollment Agreement (EA)… provides that "I understand that a student's attending the School is a privilege and not a right, and that, in all cases, the School retains the right to determine, in its sole discretion, whether or not to select a student for admission or to re-enroll a student." The [Parent-School Partnership], incorporated into the EA, allows Charlotte Latin to terminate a student's enrollment at any time, in its discretion, based on parental behavior. The termination provision reads:

A positive, collaborative working relationship between the School and a student's parent/guardians is essential to the fulfillment of the School's mission. Therefore, the School reserves the right to discontinue enrollment if it concludes that the actions of a parent/guardian make such a relationship impossible or seriously interfere with the School's mission.

Under both provisions, Charlotte Latin has broad, and indeed, near unfettered discretion to terminate a student's enrollment…. [P]rivate schools enter into contractual agreements with parents that set out terms for a child's enrollment. In forming these contractual relationships, parents and schools enjoy the freedom of contract. Parents may negotiate for different terms, including narrower termination clauses, and private schools have the right to establish their own set of rules. Parents are under no obligation to enroll their children at a particular private school—they may choose to accept the private school's contractual terms (and enroll their children) or reject the terms (and enroll their children elsewhere).

The reality is that private schools, founded on the freedom to contract and associate, are allowed to not tolerate differing viewpoints or independent thought. As long as they do not violate state or federal law or seek to enforce contracts in convention of public policy, private schools may terminate enrollments based on political ideology—and if parents are unhappy, they may exercise the right to contract with a different school that better aligns with their preferences or send their children to public schools, where the freedom to contract does not vest the school administrators with such unfettered discretion. To the extent that the complaint alleges that any reason Charlotte Latin gave for the termination was pretext, and that the children's enrollment was terminated because of "cancel culture," Charlotte Latin was allowed to do exactly that under the broad discretion it retained under the contract.

The PSP and EA expressly provided for unilateral termination at Charlotte Latin's sole discretion, whenever Charlotte Latin determined that the parent-school relationship was untenable…. Per the plain language of both the PSP and the EA, the determination of the unworkability of the parent-school relationship is entirely the school's decision to make—despite the majority's cursory attempt to distinguish Canteen, this is the same sort of unilateral authority retained by one of the contracting parties. The Turpins exercised the right to contract and agreed to abide by the termination clause in the contract when they chose to enroll their children at Charlotte Latin. In doing so, they agreed to give Charlotte Latin broad discretion over whether, when, and why to terminate their children's enrollment. The Turpins could have negotiated for a clause limiting Charlotte Latin's unilateral ability to terminate the enrollment agreement. They did not. Instead, Charlotte Latin retained the unilateral discretion to terminate the children's enrollment whenever it decided the relationship was untenable—including if it believed the Turpins' political beliefs were inconsistent with the school's values….

Whether Charlotte Latin terminated the children's enrollment because it did not like how the Turpins were communicating with the school, it disagreed with how the Turpins sought to shape curriculum to match their political beliefs, or for any other reason not prohibited by anti-discrimination laws, both the EA and PSP allowed the children's enrollment to be terminated in Charlotte Latin's sole discretion, based on Charlotte Latin's sole perception of the future tenability of the parent-school relationship. Charlotte Latin was permitted to terminate the contract whenever it decided a positive, collaborative working relationship was impossible, and it did so here, regardless of whether its proffered reason of communication was pretext for simply disliking the Turpins' views. Charlotte Latin was entitled to determine that either reason was sufficient to discontinue enrollment….

The court also allowed parents' separate fraud and defamation claims to go forward.

Christopher S. Edwards, Alex C. Dale, and Alexandra E. Ferri (Ward and Smith, P.A) and Jonathan A. Vogel (Vogel Law Firm PLLC) represent the parents.

 

The post Contract Claim Over Private School Expulsions, Allegedly Caused by Parents' Organizing Against Ideological Curriculum Changes, Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason.com.

特朗普政府正在扩大其在拉美的禁毒战争规模。

周三，国防部长彼得·赫格塞特宣布哥伦比亚将加入“美洲之盾”计划。这个多国安全联盟由美国和拉美国家组成，成立于3月份。当时，总统唐纳德·特朗普表示，该集团将致力于使用“致命的军事力量，彻底摧毁邪恶的毒贩组织和恐怖网络”。

赫格塞特表示，“美洲之盾”（即美洲反贩毒联盟）的成员将采取“具体步骤——有时是冒险的、勇敢的步骤——在合作中”实现其目标，即“拆除威胁西半球安全、稳定和主权的贩毒集团”。

至今，该地区至少有19个国家加入联盟，包括多米尼加共和国、特立尼达和多巴哥、厄瓜多尔等国。根据拉美华盛顿办公室（一家人权研究和倡导组织）的数据，这些国家的公民都曾被特朗普政府的海上特别行动击毙。

哥伦比亚加入该集团是在新总统阿贝拉多·德拉·埃斯普里耶拉的请求下。在竞选期间，埃斯普里耶拉曾承诺使用“空军、陆军和警察”摧毁所有“装满毒品的飞机和船只”，让它们永远无法离开哥伦比亚。在上周就任后，新总统立即重申承诺，告诉《华尔街日报》将“彻底击败毒贩恐怖组织和威胁哥伦比亚自由的一切犯罪组织”。

他迅速行动以兑现承诺。根据《迈阿密先驱报》报道，周日，哥伦比亚军队在全国两地的军事行动中击毙了前哥伦比亚革命武装部队的4名成员和哥伦比亚最大毒贩集团的2名成员。

在某种程度上，埃斯普里耶拉只是在延续其前任的失败政策。自2000年“哥伦比亚计划”启动以来——这是一个由美国资助的反毒计划，旨在训练、装备并协助哥伦比亚军队——美国已向哥伦比亚提供了数十亿美元的外援，但成效甚微。

去年9月，特朗普政府发现哥伦比亚“明显未能履行其毒品管制义务”，将其认定为“主要毒品过境国”和“主要非法毒品生产国之一”，这种称号已持续超过40年。据《华尔街日报》报道，哥伦比亚的可卡因产量已达到创纪录水平，“几乎是联合国研究人员估计的2012年产量的9倍”。

显然，使用军事手段打击毒品贩运从未取得显著成效，无论是对于美国还是本地区其他国家。

2025年，厄瓜多尔——该国已多年使用军事手段与毒贩作战——记录了其历史上暴力死亡人数的最高纪录。然而，非法毒品的流动却未见减少。根据《卫报》报道，目前约有70%的哥伦比亚和秘鲁生产的可卡因通过厄瓜多尔的港口流通。该国还在进口、加工和再分发合成阿片类药物的前体物方面发挥着核心作用。

该安全联盟尚未给厄瓜多尔的安全带来实际回报，但其公民为此付出了真实的代价。

1月份，中央情报局在加拉帕戈斯群岛附近的厄瓜多尔多艘渔船上实施了“秘密行动”，这是美军南部司令部海上打击行动之外的行动。根据《华盛顿邮报》报道，中央情报局的袭击导致8名厄瓜多尔国民失踪，这也是该机构在特朗普政府批准下在拉美扩大存在的一部分。3月份，美国和厄瓜多尔武装部队在联合行动中对厄瓜多尔农村的圣马丁乳制品农场进行了军事打击，结果摧毁了奶牛而非可卡因，根据《纽约时报》报道。

尽管赫格塞特的雄辩和特朗普政府对军事打击渔船的卑鄙庆祝方式，其做法只是增加了拉美地区的死伤人数，对美国流入的毒品几乎没有影响。

显然，哥伦比亚尚未从将禁毒战争军事化的失败中吸取教训，即使几十年的禁毒和禁毒政策已经失败。

本文最初发表于Reason.com。
articles.summary:
The Trump administration is expanding the footprint of its war on drugs in Latin America.

On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that Colombia would join the "Shield of the Americas" initiative. When the multinational security coalition of the U.S. and Latin American countries formed in March, President Donald Trump said the group was united by a commitment to use "lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks once and for all." 

Hegseth said members of the Shield, a.k.a. the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, will take "concrete steps—sometimes risky steps, courageous steps—in partnership" toward its goal of "dismantling the drug cartels that threaten safety, security and sovereignty in the Western Hemisphere."

To date, at least 19 countries in the region have signed on to the coalition, including the Dominican Republic, Trinidad and Tobago, and Ecuador, which have all had citizens killed by the Trump administration's extrajudicial maritime strikes, according to the Washington Office on Latin America, a human rights research and advocacy organization.

Colombia's entry into the group came at the request of its new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who on the campaign trail promised to use the "air force, the army, and the police" to neutralize every plane and boat "loaded with drugs that leaves Colombia." Moments after taking office last week, the new president doubled down, pledging to "relentlessly defeat narcoterrorism and every criminal organization that threatens Colombia's freedom," according to The Wall Street Journal. 

He has wasted no time fulfilling his promise. On Sunday, Colombian forces killed four members of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia and two members of Colombia's largest drug cartel in two military operations across the country, according to the Miami Herald.

In a way, Espriella is simply continuing the same failed policies as his predecessors. Since the launch of Plan Colombia in 2000—a counternarcotics initiative to train, equip, and assist the Colombian military financed by the U.S.—America has given Colombia billions in foreign aid, with minimal results. 

Last September, the Trump administration found Colombia had "failed demonstrably to meet its drug control obligations." It certified it as a "major drug transit" and one of the "major illicit drug producing countries," a designation it has carried for over 40 years. Cocaine production in Colombia has reached record levels, "nearly nine times what United Nations researchers say was produced in 2012," reports The Wall Street Journal. 

Clearly, using the military to fight drug trafficking has never been particularly effective, both for the U.S. and other nations in the hemisphere.

In 2025, Ecuador—which has waged a yearslong war against cartels using the military—recorded the highest number of violent deaths in its history, according to Latinoamérica21. Yet, the flow of illegal drugs continues unabated. About 70 percent of the cocaine produced in Colombia and Peru now moves through Ecuador's ports, according to The Guardian. The country also plays a central role in importing, processing, and redistributing precursors for synthetic opioids.

The security coalition has yet to yield real dividends for Ecuador's security, but it has come at real cost to its citizens. 

In January, the CIA targeted multiple Ecuadorian fishing boats near the Galápagos Islands as part of a "covert action" separate from the boat strikes by Southern Command, according to The Washington Post. The CIA strikes resulted in the disappearance of eight Ecuadorian nationals and were part of the agency's expanded presence in Latin America, sanctioned by Trump. In March, a military strike conducted as part of a joint operation between the U.S. and Ecuadorian forces destroyed a dairy farm in rural San Martín, destroying cows instead of cocaine, according to The New York Times. 

Despite Hegseth's bravado and the odious manner in which the Trump administration celebrates its military strikes on fishing boats, its approach has done nothing but increase the body count in Latin America while having a negligible effect on drugs flowing into the United States. 

Evidently, Colombia is yet to learn its lesson about militarizing the war on drugs, even after decades of interdiction and prohibition failing.

The post Colombia's New President Wants More U.S. Military Help Fighting Cartels appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: The War on Free-Range Kids Makes The New York Times
articles.content:
《纽约时报》周四的文章提出了我在这里问了十多年的问题：“让孩子独自出门是成长仪式还是犯罪？”《理性》杂志的读者都知道，在某种程度上，这两者都可能成立：一种成长仪式常常被当作犯罪来对待。作为我共同创立的非营利组织“Let Grow”的主要使命之一，我们希望确保那些给孩子一些合理独立空间的父母不会因“忽视”而遭到调查。

然而，调查仍在进行。该文章以Mallerie Shirley的故事开篇——这一故事最初由《理性》杂志报道。Shirley是亚特兰大的一位母亲，她允许6岁的儿子骑着滑板车去附近的公园。看到这一幕的某人报警，两天后，一名案件工作者出现在Shirley和丈夫Christopher Pleasants的家中。

Shirley不在家，但案件工作者（被家庭Ring摄像头记录下来）对Pleasants说，孩子必须年满13岁才能无人监督地骑自行车。Pleasants问这是否真的是法律规定。案件工作者回应称，儿童保护服务机构会认为6岁太小，“因为任何事情都可能发生，对吧？”

长期以来，这个无解的问题让政府有理由认为，任何未经监督出门（或独自待在家里）的孩子都会因为父母的疏忽而处于严重危险之中。

然而，政府并没有对孩子乘坐汽车出行抱有同样态度，尽管“任何事情都可能发生”也适用于此时。孩子每天都在车祸中丧生。权威机构也没有认为父母在让孩子吃固体食物时（什么？会窒息？）或走他们可能跌倒的楼梯时是疏忽的。允许孩子有一些无人监督的时间正成为陷阱，让好意的父母陷入困境。

该文章提到了几起父母因允许孩子单独在外活动而被捕或调查的案例：堪萨斯州、佐治亚州和马里兰州的母亲。这些故事最初由《理性》杂志报道，后来有些成为全国新闻（该文章的作者Ian Frisch还提到了我2008年写的让9岁儿子独自乘坐地铁时引发的病毒式争议）。有些案例则不为人知。然而，这些持续出现的疯狂逮捕和调查已产生影响，它改变了现状。“最终，关于儿童忽视的州法律开始改变。”Frisch写道。

制定这些“合理童年独立”法律需要付出很多努力，这些法律明确指出，“忽视”是指将孩子置于明显且严重的危险之中，而不仅仅是每当你没有看着他们的时候。目前，已有13个州通过了此类法律，另外三个州（密歇根州、俄亥俄州和宾夕法尼亚州）正在审议中，联邦层面也有一项两党协议的法律在推进。

《纽约时报》也提到了一些持异议的声音。其中一位是曾经在《每日秀》上出现的鲜明心理学家，他试图反驳独立是健康的观点。另一位是杜克大学的教授，他问道：“我们想要谨慎为上，还是想要不对父母造成麻烦？”

这是个错误的问题。被有权力夺走孩子的机构调查，绝不是小事。真正的问题是：国家是否应该有能力将偏执的育儿观点转化为法律？
articles.summary:
Thursday's edition of The New York Times asked a question I've been asking here for over a decade: "Is Letting Children Out Alone A Rite of Passage or a Crime?"

Reason readers know it can, in some sense, be both: a rite of passage too often treated as a crime. One of the primary missions of Let Grow, the nonprofit I cofounded, is to make sure the parents who trust their kids with some reasonable independence are not investigated for neglect.

But they are. The Times piece opens with the story of Mallerie Shirley—a story first reported in Reason. Shirley is an Atlanta mom who let her 6-year-old ride his scooter to the local park. Someone who saw the tyke called the authorities. Two days later a caseworker appeared at the home of Shirley and her husband, Christopher Pleasants.

Shirley wasn't home, but the caseworker (recorded on the family's Ring camera) told Pleasants that a child would have to be 13 before he could ride his bike unsupervised.

Pleasants asked if that was actually the law.

The caseworker replied that child protective services would certainly consider six too young, "because anything could happen, right?"

For too long, that unanswerable question has given the government free rein to act as if any child venturing out unsupervised (or staying home alone) is automatically in egregious danger thanks to negligent parents.

The government doesn't feel the same way about children being driven in cars, though "anything could happen" then, too. Kids are killed in car accidents every day. Nor do authorities consider parents negligent when they allow a child to eat solid food—what about choking?—or walk down stairs they could trip on. Allowing kids some unsupervised time is the net that keeps ensnaring decent parents.

The article mentions several cases of parents arrested or investigated simply for giving their kids some time outside on their own: moms in Kansas, and Georgia, and Maryland. After those stories were first reported in Reason, some went on to become national news stories. (The Times writer, Ian Frisch, also mentions my brush with viral controversy when I wrote about letting my 9-year-old riding the subway alone in 2008.) Some, meanwhile, stayed small. But the steady drip of crazy arrests and investigations has had its effect. It has moved the needle. "Eventually, state laws about child neglect began to change," Frisch writes.

It has taken a lot of effort to pass those "reasonable childhood independence" laws, which specify that "neglect" is when you put your child in obvious, serious danger—not just any time you take your eyes off them. Such laws have passed in 13 states. Three more (in Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania) are currently pending, as is a bipartisan law at the federal level.

The Times spotlights some dissenting voices. One is the same colorful psychologist featured years ago on The Daily Show who attempted to counter claims that independence is healthy. Another is a Duke professor who asks, "Do we want to err on the side of caution or do we want to err on the side of not bothering parents?"

It's the wrong question. Being investigated by the agency with the power to take away your kids is not a small bother. The real question is: Should the state have the ability to turn paranoid parenting into the law of the land?

The post The War on Free-Range Kids Makes <em>The New York Times</em> appeared first on Reason.com.
